gelangen können, der lese folgende kurze einfache und ganz wahre Darstellungen:

Es war einmal ein junger Mensch von großer Familie, der, wie es in seinem Vaterlande Sitte war, Soldat — das heißt Officier — wurde. Man stellte ihn als Fähnrich an. Er lebte mit seinen Kameraden nach ihrer Gewohnheit, mit andern Worten: er übte sich so gut, wie viele Andere, es in viehischen Ausschweifungen und Lastern so weit als möglich zu bringen. In dieser Rücksicht unternahm man zuweilen förmliche Wettkämpfe. An einem Abend befand sich der Fähnrich in Gesellschaft seiner Waffenbrüder, wo wacker gebechert wurde. Einer aus dem Kreise der allmählig lustig werdenden Brüderschaft kam auf den Einfall, man solle einmal versuchen, wer unter ihnen die größte Quantität geistiger Getränke verschlucken könne, ohne berauscht zu werden. Der Vorschlag erhielt lauten Beyfall, und man begann con Amore zu trinken, und das beliebte Getränk war — man denke! — Arrak.

Es währte, natürlich, nicht lange, so befanden sich mehrere der Zecher Sackvoll unter dem Tisch, und zu dieser Klasse gehörte der Fähnrich. Doch war das Umsinken bey weitem nicht das Final der Bacchanalien; des Fähnrichs ohnehin nicht unverwundbare Lunge hatte die drastische Flamme des Getränkes angegriffen, er wollte vor Hitze in seinen Eingeweiden erblassen, und fiel endlich in eine langwierige, schmerzhafte Brustkrankheit.

Ein verständiger Arzt rieth ihm: er solle Urlaub nehmen, aufs Land ziehen, und viel Eselsmilch trinken. Das that er, das Mittel wirkte, und er wurde so halb und halb wieder hergestellt. Nun meinte der Arzt, er solle, seiner schwachen Lunge wegen, den Militairdienst ganz quittiren, und irgend etwas anders treiben, das auf seine geschwächte Körperconstitution nicht so nachtheilig einwirke, als diese Beschäftigung. Auch dieser Rath wurde befolgt, er nahm seine Dimission, und fing aus langer Weile an, ein wenig in Kameral- und Finanzwissenschaftlichen Büchern zu blättern, so daß er am Ende in diesem Fache eine oberflächliche Idee erhielt. Seine vielgeltenden Verwandten, welche damals, als ihn der fatale Arrak aus seiner Militair-Cariere warf, ihm schiefe Gesichter schnitten, wurden nun wieder freundlich, und beschlossen auf der Stelle, aus ihm etwas Rechtes im Civil zu schaffen. Da er alle hebenden Vorzüge, als Geld, Erbadel und Protection seiner hohen Familie, besaß, so konnte es gar nicht fehlen. Man stellte ihn vortheilhaft an, als er sich kaum gemeldet hatte, und stieg von Amt zu Amt immer höher empor, bis zum angesehensten und bedeutendsten Staatsbeamten, der sogar einen Orden trug.

Ein Andrer flog schnell im Militair eine Stufe nach der andern hinan, weil eine Hofdame, als er noch Sekondlieutenant war, zur Gemahlin des Fürsten von ihm sagte: Gestern habe ich mit dem N. N. getanzt. „D,

Kann man nun wohl mehr verlangen, als daß der Tanz hier, und dort der Arrak zu Aemtern und Würden führt?

Ueber die Tendenz der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse des preußischen Hofes ꝛc. und des Journals: Neue Feuerbrände.

Es ist wohl Zeit, daß der Verfasser der ersten, und der Redakteur der letztern sich darüber laut erklärt, da so manche Recensenten darnach gefragt haben, denen die Fassungsgabe fehlt; denn sonst müßten es ihnen jene Werke wohl eingetrichtert haben.

Diese Recensenten haben auch gesagt: man müsse vorher einen Fehler rügen, nicht nachher, und die Briefe wären nicht von 1786 her, sondern erst ganz neuerlich geschrieben, und was des Gesagten mehr ist.

Meinetwegen mögen sie sagen, die Herren, was sie wollen, es ist mir völlig einerlei; denn sie habens nur immer mit der Form und mit Titeln, Druckfehlern, und was weiß ich womit zu thun.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 124
text:
Da aber jene Werke stark gelesen werden, und dieser oder jener zweifelhaft seyn möchte, ob es gut gethan sey, mit freyer Stirn die Fehler seiner vaterländischen Verfassung aufzudecken, so sehe ich mich veranlaßt, darüber mich näher zu erklären:

So lange wie ein Staat, schwach im Innern, von Außen durch seinen blendenden Schein den Nachbaren noch imponirt, so lange ist es Pflicht des Patrioten, seine Schwächen nicht aufzudecken; er mag dann im Stillen wirken, rathen, warnen — helfen, wo er kann. Ob ich das redlich gethan habe? darüber kann ich mich hier nicht erklären. Selbst Napoleon, der alles weiß, kannte doch nicht so unsere Schwäche, als er sie nachher fand. Dies beweist seine Anrede an die Truppen vor dem 14. Octbr., dies beweisen seine Worte:

> Certainement ils se tromperont ces perruques!

und auf dem Napoleonsberge:

> Les prussiens sont encore plus stupides que les autrichiens,

als er ihre verworrene Position erblickte.

Wer also dann öffentlich auftritt, wie Bälov in seinem Feldzuge 1805, der bringt nur seiner Eitelkeit ein Opfer; er verdient sich zwar den Namen eines Propheten,

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 125
text:
aber er hat dem Feinde die Schwäche des Staats verrathen.

Wenn aber nichts mehr zu verschweigen ist, wenn der Staat in Trümmern zerschlagen daliegt; wenn die Ersten des Landes sich als Verräther, Poltrons und Dummköpfe brandmarken (fehlt es etwa daran?); wenn der König verlassen da steht; wenn der größte Theil des gebildeten vaterländischen Publikums, verzweifelnd an der Wiederherstellung des Staats, sich dem Feinde hinwirft, ihm Treue schwört, ihm das Staats-Eigenthum verräth, ihm diejenigen nennt, die es noch redlich mit dem geschlagenen, verlassenen Könige meynen; wenn eine Menge von Beamten schaamlos sich bereichert, denen die Ausschreibung der Armeebedürfnisse des Feindes überlassen worden ist, so ist es wohl Zeit, daß eine Stimme in der Wüsten erschalle, und dem besser gesinnten Publikum die Ursachen des zertrümmerten Staats begreiflich mache, auf die Elenden mit Fingern zeige, die Schuld daran sind, die Schurken brandmarke, die weiter nichts begreifen, als was ihre Taschen füllt. Es ist wohl löblich, wenn man auf der andern Seite die Edlen in der Nation nennt, die ihre Pflicht thaten, und wohl noch mehr?

Schändlich ist der Vorwurf in den Zeiten (ich meyne das Journal): Man schildere den König sehr gut, damit seine Schwäche desto mehr hervorleuchte.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 126
text:
Es müßte wohl ein eben so elender Schmeichler und Speichellecker seyn, als jener Kritiker — ein hämischer Recensent ist, der mit elenden Advokatenkniffen sich brüstet, der vom Könige sagen könnte:

> Er ist ein großer Kopf, ein zweyter Friedrich, ein großer Feldherr u. s. w.

Der König ist ein guter moralischer Mensch, hat einen gesunden Menschenverstand, und leistet, was er leisten kann.

Was soll man mehr von ihm verlangen? Dadurch, daß ich das gesagt habe, kann ich ihm das Zutrauen der Nation nicht nehmen, sondern ich suche es zu erhalten.

Andere meynen: Enthielten die Briefe und die neuen Feuerbrände auch Wahrheiten, so kämen sie doch zur unrechten Zeit. Eine Sonne die bloß leuchte, aber nicht erwärme!

Ich möchte doch einmal sehen, wie es mit dem Erwärmen zugehen sollte?

Das meynen die Herren so hinter dem warmen Ofen. Sie sollten aber einmal hinaustreten unters Volk, da würden sie bald merken, daß es mit allem Erwärmen am Ende sey: Das ist alles vergebens!

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 127
text:
Es muß jetzt niedergerissen und niedergebrannt werden, was an Mißbräuchen jetzt entblößt dasteht; es müssen die Staatsverräther öffentlich gebrandmarkt und bestraft werden; der König muß sich mit den Edelsten (nicht etwa Adel) umgeben, um aus dem alten Wust etwas Gehaltvolles aufzubauen.

Darum die Briefe! darum die neuen Feuerbrände!

Ich werde übrigens es nicht dulden, daß jemand Unrecht geschähe, und wenn es ohne meine Schuld geschehen ist, so soll es berichtigt werden.

Jetzt höre ich noch manche Stimme, welche mir zuruft: Welchen Verfolgungen setzest du dich aus? Wie wird man dich verläumden, wenn der König zurückkommt! Man wird dir den Prozeß machen, dich einkerkern, richten und beschimpfen.

Daran kehre ich mich sehr wenig. Nennen werde ich mich dem Könige, Er, der Gerechte, mag über mich richten. Geduldig werde ich meinen Nacken jeder Strafe hinhalten, mein Trost wird dann seyn: Daß der Buchstabe nicht erlöscht.

Kann man Anhänger des wahren ächten preußischen Staatssystems richten und bestrafen, so ist dies der größte Beweis, daß es nicht mehr existirt.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 128
text:
Soviel über die Tendenz meiner Schriften, und nun laßt mich damit in Ruhe, ihr Recensionen-Fabrikanten, und ihr Schwächlinge, die ihr nicht Muth habt, in die Schranken zu treten, und die ihr lieber den Feinden Weihrauch streut (der ihnen anekelt), damit sie euch eure paar Thaler Gehalt auszahlen.

Die Redaktion der neuen Feuerbrände.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 129
text:
Erklärung des Verfassers der vertrauten Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse des preußischen Hofes ꝛc. das schwarze Register im zweyten Hefte der neuen Feuerbrände betreffend.

Auf dem Titel des ersten Heftes der neuen Feuerbrände stehe ich mit Recht als Herausgeber; denn bis auf den letzten Aufsatz von Benkowitz sind alle von mir selbst.

Der zweyte Heft enthält nur die Abhandlung Seite 118 von mir. Dieses Heft ist mir nicht eher zu Gesicht gekommen, als da ich eben von einer zweymonatlichen Reise zurückkam. Die Aufsätze sind daher vor dem Druck nicht von mir gelesen worden.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 130
text:
Ich finde nun in diesem Hefte das schwarze Register, und fühle mich berufen, hierdurch zu erklären, daß jenes Register Wahrheit und Lügen durch einander mengt, den Stempel der Animosität und Gemeinheit trägt. Es wird darin geschimpft und gelästert, wodurch niemand der Wahrheit und Gerechtigkeit eine Stütze giebt. Der Verfasser hat sich nicht genannt; das Manuscript ist durch die dritte Hand an den Verleger der neuen Feuerbrände eingesandt, das Publikum wird ihn aber leicht an dem Titel, an der Form und an der Tendenz erkennen. Er mag sein Machwerk verantworten.

Er mag mit so vielen rechten, die in diesem Register compromittirt und verläumdet sind; er mag es verantworten, daß grade jetzt diese Schmähschrift erscheint, und vielleicht Veranlassung wird, das Unglück mancher Familie zu begründen, wenn der Staat diese Schenkungen wieder einzieht, die sich zum Theil schon in der dritten Hand befinden.

Ich vertheidige die gerügten Donationen nicht, ich habe meine Meynung darüber im ersten Theil der vertrauten Briefe gesagt. Wenn es gewiß ist, daß der Graf Hoym gegen die Einziehung der geistlichen Güter und Starosteyen protestirte, wie kann er die Donationen eingeleitet haben?

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 131
text:
Doch ich will die Unrichtigkeiten, welche mir nur in dem schwarzen Register bekannt sind, rügen, darnach mag das Publikum das Ganze beurtheilen.

S. 67. No. 7. Stadtpräsident Eisenberg in Berlin.

Nach dem Aufruhr in Breslau mußte Eisenberg nach Breslau reisen und die Sache untersuchen. Hoym fiel vor ihm auf die Knie, und bat ihn um Gotteswillen, ihn nicht unglücklich zu machen, daher diese Schenkung.

Die Unwahrheit dieser Schmähung geht aus sich selbst hervor. Wer den Graf Hoym kennt, der begreift es sogleich, daß es ihm physisch und moralisch unmöglich ist:

> Auf die Knie zu fallen.

Wie hätte der lahme Mann das möglich machen sollen?

Unter allen Umständen hatte die Klugheit Hoyms Resourcen genug, sich einer solchen erniedrigenden Handlung gegen einen Eisenberg zu überheben. Die Schuld, den Aufruhr veranlaßt zu haben, fiel auf Werner,

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 132
text:
dem Stadtpräsidenten in Breslau, einen unmittelbaren Günstling Friedrich Wilhelm II., dem er als Kronprinz Gelder negociirt hatte.

S. 69. Fürst Hohenloh.

Der Tausch, den Hohenloh zwischen dem Amte Crotozcyn und seinen Donationen vorschlug, wäre nicht ungerecht gewesen, wenn er nach den Anschlägen geschah, welche von beyden Tauschobjekten gemacht wurden. Der Staatsminister von Voß vereitelte dies Projekt, vielleicht aus guter Absicht. Dem Könige dienten aber die Hohenlohschen Besitzungen mehr, wie Crotozcyn; denn sie arondirten, so viele der südpreußischen Aemter, von denen sie unklugerweise abgerissen waren.

S. 71. Der Graf Lüttichau.

Dem Regierungsrath von Grevenitz geschieht hier zu viel; er wird hier geradezu der Bestechung beschuldigt.

Grevenitz war ja gar nicht Richter in der Sache, sondern der officielle Beystand der Gräfin Gurovska; auch ist der Rechtsstreit der Gurovskyschen Eheleute quo ad Bona gar nicht abgeurtheilt, sondern verglichen worden. (Man sieht, wie schlecht der Verfasser

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 133
text:
unterrichtet war.) Alle hier angegebnen Summen sind falsch. Was hier von dem Justizrath Reinhard steht, ist ganz unwahr.

S. 75.

Hoym hat Murowanna Goslin für 120000 Rthlr. gekauft, und um eben den Preis verkauft.

Wenn der Kauf von ihm aus Gefälligkeit gegen Bischofswerder geschehen wäre, wie würde er so unklug gewesen seyn, sogleich an 40 Procent daran zu verdienen? Man sieht, wie sehr den Verfasser die Wuth zu schmähen hingerissen, und wie inkonsequent er dabey verfahren hat.

S. 76.

Der Ritterschaftsrath von Unruh ist ein so rechtschaffner Mann, wie der General Köckeritz, und es ist nicht wahr, daß die benannten Güter dem letztern geschenkt wären, sondern sie sind dem von Unruh in Erbenzinß gegen ein Erbstandsgeld und Abfindung des vorigen Besitzers, Grafen Lucas v. Bninsky, verliehen worden. Diese Abfindung hat Hr. v. Unruh theuer bezahlen, und überdies das auf den Gütern gefundene Inventarium mit Gelde aufwiegen müssen. Er hat die

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 134
text:
Gebäude, die verwahrlost waren, in Stand gesetzt, und manche Melioration gemacht, ehe er sie verkaufte.

S. 83.

Unter der Taxe der Triebenfeldschen Güther und ihrem Verkaufspreise, stecken seine ihm eigenthümlich gehörigen Güter.

---

Es sey genug an diesen Berichtigungen, die mir entfernt von den Quellen jetzt nur einfallen.

Mit dem vierten Hefte geht die Redaktion einzig und allein durch meine Hände, und alsdann stehe ich für jeden Aufsatz in den neuen Feuerbränden.

Der dritte Hefte war bis auf diesen Nachsatz auch schon gedruckt.

---

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 135
text:
Note des Verlegers.

Ich muß es der Wahrheit gemäß anerkennen, daß der Verf. der vertrauten Briefe von dem Druck des schw. Reg. nichts gewußt hat; ich meldete ihm dessen Eingang: allein mein Brief verfehlte ihn, indem er schon abgereist war. Er erhielt ihn endlich, und antwortete sogleich:

„Hüten Sie sich für diesen Aufsatz; das schwarze Register ist mir als Manuscript bekannt, es enthält viele Unrichtigkeiten, es ist besonders gegen den Grafen Hoym gerichtet. Ich will an allen Schmähungen gegen diesen Greis keinen Theil haben, um so weniger als er jetzt außer Dienst [illegible]. Mag der Graf Hoym Schwächen haben, er war dennoch einer der klügsten preußischen Minister.“

Diese Antwort kam zu spät, das zweyte Heft der neuen Feuerbrände war bereits in alle Welt.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft

S. 108. 3te Zeile v. o. lies, statt Napoleon werde ihn zum Kammerdirektor erheben: der König werde ihn einst zum Kammerdirektor erheben.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 137
text:
Antwort auf ein anonymes Schreiben des Verfertigers des schwarzen Registers.

Es ist an die Redaktion der Neuen Feuerbrände ein Schreiben des schwarzen Registrators eingegangen, worin dem von ihm vermutheten Verfasser der vertrauten Briefe mancherley Schuld gegeben wird, was wir hier öffentlich beantworten wollen. Es heißt darin:

Mir ist in keinem Sinne ein Gefallen damit geschehen, daß Sie meine Tabelle von den südpreußischen Donationen in dem Zweyten Hefte der Neuen Feuerbrände haben abdrucken lassen.

Dem jetzigen Redakteur und Verfasser der vertrauten Briefe noch weit weniger; mit seinem Willen steht diese Tabelle nicht in den Neuen Feuerbränden. Es liegen noch Bruchstücke aus den Proceß-Akten eines Herrn v. d vor uns, welche auch an die Redaktion eingesandt worden, deren Schriftzüge außerordentliche Aehnlichkeit mit denen jenes Anschreibens haben. Wir werden keinen Gebrauch davon machen.

Ich gehöre nicht zu den Poltrons; aus Gründen, die ich hier zu entwickeln nicht Lust habe, werde ich vielleicht öffentlich gegen Sie schweigen, auf Ihre Kosten aber werde ich privatim mit sehr derber Darstellung

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 138
text:
Ihres Charakters mich rechtfertigen, wenn das Geschwader der Donatarien mir Verdruß erregen wollte, ob schon Sie den Lobredner jener Leute machen.

Das kann der schwarze Herr Registrator halten wie er will, er muß wissen, wem er sein Register abgelassen hat; ob er mich übrigens von vorne oder von hinten anfallen will, das gilt mir gleich, da ich auf allen Seiten gegen ihn gewaffnet bin.

So wenig ich den Inhalt jener skandalösen Tabelle widerrufen werde, so muß ich doch jetzt gegen die unzeitige Publizirung protestiren; ich halte es für unedel eine unglückliche Regierung zu beschimpfen.

Darin hat der Herr Briefsteller sehr recht. Ist ihm aber sein Register entwandt worden? der Verleger versichert es doch aus soliden Händen erhalten zu haben. Sollte der Herr Verfasser es nicht irgendwo communizirt haben?

Ich habe einen Theil meiner Ideen — Urtheile (nur freylich mit etlichen Schmeicheleyen ausstaffirt) in den vertrauten Briefen wieder gefunden.

Daß ich nicht wüßte. Wollten der Herr Briefschreiber sich nur nicht zu viel einbilden. Freylich würden Hochdieselben eine andere Charakteristik des preußischen Hofes geschrieben haben, wie ich.

Es ist eine offenbare Lüge, wenn Sie in den vertrauten Briefen sagen: Ich sauge aus allen Dingen Gift.

Bezeugt dies nicht etwa das schwarze Register?

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 139
text:
Spott und Tadel haben in mir jederzeit eine moralische Tendenz. Ihre eigenen Schriften enthalten ja Materialien in Menge zur Rechtfertigung meiner Prophezeyungen, nur mit dem Unterschiede, daß Sie allemal zurücktreten, wenn es darauf ankommt, personel zu verfahren, ich aber frisch auf die Personen losstürme u. s. w.

Daran thun Sie sehr übel, mein Herr!

Ich habe nichts mit den Personen, alles mit den Sachen zu thun: der rechtschaffenste Mann kann die verderblichsten Projekte ausführen, indem er sie für gut hält: Exempl. grat. Herr Baron v. Stein und die Tresorscheine!

Welchen Nutzen könnten Sie stiften, und in welchem edlen Lichte stünden Sie da, wenn Ihr Charakter von eben so reinem Metall und Ihre Tugend so fest wäre, wie Ihre Kenntnisse umfassend und Ihre Einsichten meist richtig sind.

Kann denn der Herr Registrator so bestimmt wissen, daß Derjenige, an den er seinen Brief schrieb, der Verfasser der vertrauten Briefe ist?

Uebrigens besteht die Tugend nicht in Beschimpfungen der Personen, die die Staatsangelegenheiten leiten. Man hält sich an Diese, nicht an Jene, und wenn der Verfasser im zweyten Theil diese Regel manchmal verlassen hat, so thut es ihm jetzt leid.

Man sieht: Es ist nicht Allen, Alles Recht zu machen.

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3
label: Part 3, p. 140
text:
Sie, der Lobredner und Partisan Hoyms, Sie publiciren meine Güthertabelle!

Das wäre freylich eine große Inconsequenz, wenn es nur wahr wäre!

Ich werde aber trotz Ihrer Schimpfreden, mein Herr Registrator, der Lobredner des Graf Hoyms bleiben, und vergessen Sie nicht, daß er außer Diensten ist, mir also weder nützen noch schaden kann. Ich würde hinzusetzen: Er kenne mich nicht; wenn Sie sich belehren ließen.

Das verdrüßlichste ist, daß die Güther-Tabelle nicht nur nicht nach einem unvollständigen Manuscript, worin vieles gefehlt hat, abgedruckt worden ist, sondern (hier bekomme ich wieder einen Verweis) auch Verwirrungen darin geschehen sind.

Das Publikum sieht also: jenes schwarze Register ist nicht ächt. Ich mag weiter nichts damit zu thun haben.

Mag meinetwegen der Herr Registrator nun ein ächtes drucken lassen, oder jenes widerrufen, oder ausmitteln, wer hinter seinem Rücken das Manuscript verkauft hat, das ist mir alles einerley.

---

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3

text:
Anzeige.

So eben ist nun vollendet

Heinrich Brosenius 
Technologie

Lehrer in Schulen

Erster und zweyter Band.

75½ Bogen Text und 9 Kupfertafeln in 4to. 
Leipzig 1807, bey Heinrich Gräff. 
Verkaufspreis 3 Thlr. Partie-Preis bey 6 Exempl. à 2 Thlr.

Wenn es wahr ist, daß von allen Kenntnissen die practischen, oder die, welche in unmittelbarer Beziehung mit dem practischen Leben stehen, die wichtigsten und unerläßlichsten sind, so gehören technische Kenntnisse, nach dem einstimmigen Urtheile aller Erzieher, zu den unentbehrlichsten, und so ist es gewiß richtig, was der Verfasser jenes Werks in der Vorrede zum ersten Bande sagt: „daß Jeder, der Anspruch auf Bildung macht, von der Technologie ohngefähr so viel, als in seiner Schrift enthalten ist, wissen müsse, wenn er nicht oft in Verlegenheit gesetzt seyn wolle, traurige Blößen zu geben.“ — Man kann daher dieses Werk ohne Bedenken als ein unentbehrliches Stück in jeder, wenn auch noch

title: Neue Feuerbrände. Marginalien zu der Schrift: Vertraute Briefe über die innern Verhältnisse am Preußischen Hofe seit dem Tode Friedrichs II. Erster Band, erstes bis drittes Heft
title_en: New Firebrands. Marginalia on the Tract: Confidential Letters on the Internal Affairs of the Prussian Court since the Death of Frederick II. First volume, parts 1 to 3

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 266
text:
9 The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795

Robert I. Frost

University of Aberdeen

I

> We live in the present, we know not the future: possessions are nothing but accidental, subject to all kinds of vagaries; but Nobility is eternal.

Even for a sophisticated Frenchman like Jean le Laboureur, visiting Poland in 1645, the noble society of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was impressive enough to stimulate philosophical awe. In a Europe dominated so completely by noble élites, the Commonwealth was the noble state par excellence. Foreigners marvelled at what the Irishman Bernard Connor termed the ‘extraordinary Grandeur of the Nobility’, which enjoyed unparalleled powers and privileges:

> the Polish Nation is divided into two sorts of People, the Gentry or Free-born Subjects, who are hardly a tenth Part of the Kingdom, and the Vassals, who are no better than Slaves to the Gentry, for they have no Benefit of the Laws, can buy no Estates, nor Enjoy any Property, no more than our Negroes in the West-Indies can.

Though this was an exaggeration, the extent of noble power certainly seemed impressive. Already by the early sixteenth century, the Polish szlachta (nobility) was a legally defined Estate, with extensive privileges at law. In 1374, it was exempted from ordinary taxation on hereditary noble land without its explicit consent. By the principle of neminem captivabimus nisi iure victum, accepted by the monarchy in 1433, no nobleman could be imprisoned unless formally convicted of a crime. The 1496 privileges of Piotrków banned non-nobles from acquiring landed estates, gave the nobility wide economic privileges and restricted peasant mobility; the legal basis of

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 267
text:
serfdom was formally completed by Sigismund I's 1518 grant to the nobility of full jurisdiction over its serfs.

Gradually, the szlachta established control of the political system. The need for noble consent to taxation required the gathering of the nobility in the local sejmiki (dietines). From 1454, the king could not summon the nobility to perform its military duty in the general levy (pospolite ruszenie) without the agreement of the sejmiki, which were henceforth to scrutinize all new legislation. To facilitate the conduct of business, a bicameral Sejm (Diet) was established in the 1490s, consisting of the Senate – comprising Catholic bishops, government ministers and the palatines and castellans who were the chief provincial officials – and the Chamber of Envoys, composed of delegates (usually two) from each sejmik. By the statute of Nihil Novi (1505) all new legislation had to be passed by the Sejm. Following the parliamentary union of the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania at Lublin in 1569, the Sejm became exclusively noble. On the extinction of the Jagiellonian dynasty in the male line in 1572, the right of all nobles to participate in royal elections was institutionalized; henceforward the election of the monarch viritim was regarded as the fundamental guarantee of noble liberty. Finally, the nobility took control of its own judicial affairs with the establishment of separate tribunals in Poland (1578) and Lithuania (1581) as supreme appellate courts for cases involving nobles, in which judges were elected by the nobility, not appointed by the king. These three developments extended noble control over the executive, legislative and judicial functions of the state. According to Laboureur, ‘There is no more true Nobility in the world than that of this Kingdom; there is none also which enjoys such advantageous privileges.’

By 1600 Poland-Lithuania seemed to be – and was seen to be – a state run by nobles for the nobles. Indeed, it was the extent of power and privilege won by the Polish szlachta which helped persuade Lithuanian nobles to accept political union against the opposition of a small group of magnates. From 1569, powerful forces of cultural integration operated among the noble élites of Poland and Lithuania, coalescing round a shared vision of a state based on the perfect coincidence of citizenship with noble status. This was justified by a heady mixture of classical political theory, whose principles were adapted to match a noble-dominated political system, with an elaborate justification of this monopoly through the creation of a mythical common past and identity for the new Commonwealth's ruling class. This identity-myth claimed that the szlachta, whether of Polish, Lithuanian, Ruthenian or German descent, formed one political nation, descended from the ancient Sarmatian tribe which had long resisted the Roman Empire. By the mid-seventeenth century, the hallmarks of the ‘Sarmatian nation’ were the use of the Polish language, adherence to the Catholic faith and the adoption of a distinctive style of dress, heavily influenced by Turkic and Tatar models, which symbolized the difference between the Polish constitution and the

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 268
text:
political systems of Western Europeans, whose effete, mincing fashions were taken to denote the domination of society by absolute royal power.

Although the szlachta enjoyed, in theory at least, a greater degree of social and political power than nobles elsewhere in Europe, nobility was defined in essentially similar terms. Szymon Starowolski (1588–1653), from a poor Volhynian noble background, who rose to be a canon of Cracow Cathedral, wrote that

> The Polish people is first divided into the equestrian order, or the nobility, and the common people; secondly into the ecclesiastic and lay orders. The nobility is distinguished for the purpose of government and defence, the common people for agriculture, mercantile and mechanical pursuits: on the other hand, the priests are dedicated to the worship of GOD.

Marcin Kromer (1512–89), Bishop of Warmia, stressed the importance of virtue, of living in a noble fashion, of land ownership, and of descent:

> The Polish nobility separated itself off for the government and defence of the rest of the people and of the country. Thus those who form this estate in former times were called knights and now – because of their duty to provide service as cavalrymen – are most frequently called equites, by those who speak and write Latin; in the mother tongue, however, they are called shliahta, from the szlachetność (nobility) of their family – in which, if I am not mistaken, the word was borrowed from the German (Geschlechter) – and ziemianie (the landed ones) or, as it is commonly explained, terrigene. This name comes from the lands and fields which they till and where they have lived so long, which they inherit, buy or are granted by the prince.

The rationalization of the nobility's privileged position, and the idealizations of noble life offered by poets and political theorists were, therefore, highly conventional: nobility was essentially transmitted by descent, having originally been earned for the services rendered by a noble's forebears. Since nobility was in origin a reward for virtue and service, especially military service, nobles could be created, although nobles by birth enjoyed greater status than those who had been born commoners. A nobleman was expected to maintain a noble lifestyle and perform the functions proper to his station: he was to live as a gentleman, to be based on the land and to defend the fatherland in time of danger; indeed, the legal requirement to serve in the general levy survived into the eighteenth century.

Nowhere in Europe was a nobility so unrestricted in its ability to make the letter of the law match a view of society based on noble supremacy. A 1505 statute decreed that a noble must demonstrate szlachta descent on his

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 269
text:
maternal as well as his paternal side; from 1578 the law required that the Sejm ratify all new noble creations, to curb royal initiative and to block the selling of noble status by the Crown. The extent of noble domination might suggest that the Commonwealth's governing élite was a stable and static class which, having apparently reduced the monarchy to a cipher and the peasantry to what Connor and other foreign observers perceived as abject servitude, had complete control over its own position, status and membership. Yet reality was very different from theory and, despite the clearly defined legal framework, the conventional idealization of the nobility, and the spread of Sarmatism in the seventeenth century, the Commonwealth's ruling élite was anything but a homogeneous class, and proved to be both volatile and highly unstable. Much of the apparent control was illusory, and the period from 1569 to 1795 saw constant changes within this élite, ending with the collapse from within of the noble nation and a fundamental redefinition of nobility itself.

II

The Sarmatian myth claimed a common origin for the whole szlachta, but the assertion of a common identity could not conceal that the Commonwealth was a State whose component parts, each with its own traditions and social structure, had only recently come together. By the thirteenth century a noble Estate with clear legal privileges, composed of the landed, warrior class, had emerged within the medieval Kingdom of Poland. The influence of the Latin civilization of western Europe was strong: many Polish terms for the ordo equestris (knightly Estate) came from German via Czech, including szlachta itself, and herb (coat-of-arms) from the German Erbe (inheritance). Yet while the Polish nobility shared many characteristics with the nobilities of Hungary and Bohemia, it acquired particular features of its own as a result of Poland's political development.

Originally, there had been various groups among the military entourages of the earliest Polish princes, and a distinction between those referred to as nobiles, who enjoyed greater privileges, and the simple rycerze or milites (knights). Already by the twelfth century the initial practice of temporary, revocable grants of land by princes to both nobiles and milites was giving way to the establishment of hereditary ownership. Despite the widely differing economic and social positions within the broad categories of nobiles and milites, several factors prevented the solidifying of a feudal hierarchy. From the eleventh century, the practice of conferring knighthood on a wide range of members of the landed-warrior class spread rapidly. The custom of partible inheritance acted against the entrenchment of the economic power of the upper nobility, not least because it all but caused the permanent break-up of the state when Bolesław the Wrymouth divided his kingdom on his death in 1138. His descendants, in their separate duchies, sought to consolidate their

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 270
text:
power through the mass granting of various immunities to all nobles, high and low, who held land iure militari (by military law). This trend reached its peak in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth century, as Władysław Łokietek struggled to reunite the Polish state, which he ruled as king from 1320. The death of Władysław's son, Casimir the Great (1333–70), without a male heir – although it did not lead to the break-up of the kingdom – ensured that the nobility was able to maintain and extend the privileges it had won while central authority had been weak.

By the mid-fourteenth century, any trend towards a feudal hierarchy had been decisively reversed. Immunities and privileges were granted to the szlachta as a whole: nobilitas was now taken to apply to all who possessed land iure militari and who could, according to statutes passed under Casimir the Great, demonstrate noble descent. Even those who did not own land, but were noble by descent – the szlachta nieosiadła or impossessionati – were regarded as nobles, even if they did not enjoy all the privileges of the Estate. This trend towards equality of treatment was consolidated in the great wave of privileges granted by Casimir's successors after 1370 as the price of recognition as king. The emergence of noble clans, comprising groups of noble families of differing status under a common coat-of-arms as a focus of identity, encouraged the idea that the nobility was one estate with common privileges: adoption into a clan remained a way into the nobility until the sixteenth century.

Despite this trend, the nobility remained highly diverse, reflecting differences between the kingdom's component provinces. The influence of magnates was greater in Little Poland than in Great Poland, where the middle and petty nobility was both numerous and powerful. Royal Prussia came under the Polish Crown after the Thirteen Years War against the Teutonic Knights (1454–66). It only began sending official envoys to the Sejm in 1569, and it maintained its own political structure into the eighteenth century. The continuing importance of the great trading cities of Danzig, Elbing and Thorn meant that the nobility was never in as dominant a position as elsewhere: representatives of these three cities sat in the Senate of the Prussian Landtag (the only bicameral sejmik in the Commonwealth), and the lesser cities sent envoys to the lower house until 1662. The duchy of Mazovia, part of the Polish state until 1138, was only reincorporated in 1529; it remained the heartland of the petty nobility. The dukes of Mazovia, engaged in constant battles with the pagan Prussian and Lithuanian tribes, had encouraged settlement of the forest wastelands which made up so much of their duchy by liberally distributing charters of nobility to colonists, whose numerous descendants defended their noble status with tenacity: so numerous were they that Bartłomiej Paprocki, who published his Coats of Arms of the Polish Nobility in 1584, gave up in despair when he came to Mazovia.

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 271
text:
III

If the influence of the Latin civilization of Western Europe was strong in the development of the Polish nobility, the nobility of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, while increasingly open to western ideas and concepts, emerged from a more distinctly eastern tradition, in which military service lay at the heart of the system. From the thirteenth century the Grand Dukes of Lithuania ruled vast tracts of sparsely populated territory including the Lithuanian heartland round Wilno and Troki and much of the western Ruthenian lands (present-day Belarus and Ukraine) which came under Lithuanian rule after the collapse of Kievan Rus in the face of the Mongol onslaughts of the thirteenth century. Constant warfare against the Tatars, the pagan tribes of the Baltic coastlands, the Teutonic Knights who sought to subdue them, and various eastern Slavic princes meant that the transformation from a military to a landed estate took rather longer than in Poland.

The Grand Duchy before the 1386 Union with Poland was an uneasy amalgam of pagan Lithuanians and Orthodox eastern Slavs. The influence of east Slavic culture was strong: since Orthodox clergymen were probably the only literate members of society, Old Court Ruthenian – an ancestor of modern Belorussian and Ukrainian – became the official language. Western influences, however, were always important, through contacts with Poland and the Teutonic Knights. By the fourteenth century, the sources describe the élites of Lithuanian society in various ways: in Latin as nobiles, nobiliores, satrapae, potentiores, barones, meliores; an individual might be known as shliaikhtich, from the Polish szlachcic, or in eastern terms as kniaz or boiar. Quite what these terms meant in practice is not always easy to determine. East-Slavic influences remained strong: the importance of princely blood was recognized, and descendants of the houses of Gedymin, the Lithuanian ruling dynasty, and Rurik, which had ruled Kievan Rus, were entitled to use the title kniaz (prince, duke). The Grand Duke maintained a small council of high nobles; otherwise, there were various ranks of servitors, who might be bonded men, free peasants or enjoy the greater privileges of the zemianin – a member of the military service class.

It was in the context of the growing political relationship with Poland from the late fourteenth century that a noble Estate in the western sense began to develop. Lithuania, facing fierce challenges from the Teutonic Knights and from Muscovy, increasingly looked to Poland for military support. After the Lithuanian Grand Duke Jogaila (1377–1434) converted to Catholicism, taking the name Władysław Jagiełło, to become King of Poland in 1386, he wooed the pagan Lithuanian boyars into adopting the Catholic faith in 1387 by granting them certain privileges, the most important of which, for the creation of a true landed nobility, was the removal of service obligations on private estates and the introduction of rights of inheritance. Nevertheless, the 1387 privilege does not appear to have been fully implemented,

title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 272
text:
and the exact status of individual estates and of individual members of the Lithuanian élites was still unclear: the extent of service obligations continued to vary widely and the situation was complicated by the fact that the great Lithuanian and Ruthenian magnates maintained military servitors of their own, to whom they granted land in return for service, when required, in their own military retinues. The uncertainty of Lithuania's political status after 1386 and growing Polish influence, however, gave some – but not all – lesser groups among the landed-service élites the opportunity to win an ever greater degree of privilege and control over their affairs.

For most of the fifteenth century, Lithuania was governed by various members of the Jagiellonian dynasty, while the head of the family assumed the Crown in Cracow. As ideas concerning noble rights and privileges entered from Poland, and the de facto rulers of Lithuania starting with Vytautas (Witold), Jagiełło's cousin, Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1392 to 1430, sought to maintain control by buying off political support, the position of the Lithuanian landed élites began to change. At the Union of Horodło in 1413, hereditary rights over certain estates were reaffirmed for Catholic boyars, and 47 leading Lithuanian families were ‘adopted' by Polish noble clans, assuming their coats-of-arms. Over the next 150 years, these privileges were gradually extended to wider strata of the military-landed élite. From the very outset the conversion to Catholicism of the leading Lithuanian boyars and the failure to include Orthodox Ruthenians among those granted privileges after 1387 threatened to blow the fragile state apart. Ruthenian boyars displayed growing hostility to Vytautas, which erupted into civil war on his death, fought between Śvitrigaila Algirdaitis, a younger brother of Jagiełło, and Žyigimantas Kestutaitis, a younger brother of Vytautas. Śvitrigaila allied with the Teutonic Knights and courted Ruthenian support; although he was ultimately defeated, the victorious Žyigimantas was forced to extend equal privileges to Ruthenian boyars in 1434 as the price of peace.

Although some Ruthenians still looked east, and there was a degree of support for political union with Muscovy until the mid-seventeenth century, from the 1430s the growing attraction of the Polish model of extensive noble privileges brought the élites of Poland and Lithuania ever closer, especially against the background of developments in Muscovy, where the behaviour of Ivan the Terrible (1533–84) created a negative image of Muscovite power which lasted deep into the seventeenth century. As the autonomy of the high nobles was steadily reduced during the fifteenth century, there was a series of defections of Ruthenian magnates to Muscovy, but the growing attraction of noble privileges granted on the Polish model restricted the appeal of that route; while the position of the Muscovite dvorianstvo remained uncertain and dominated by the service ethic, their Lithuanian counterparts began to flourish.

From the fifteenth century, estates of the Grand Duchy's leading nobles grew in size as the rights and privileges of the nobility were codified in the

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 273
text:
general land privileges of 1447, 1492 and 1506, and in the three Lithuanian Statutes of 1529, 1566 and 1588. The privileges of 1492 and 1506 agreed that the prince could decide nothing new without the agreement of his council, but the growing power of the magnates was matched by the political assertiveness of the middling Lithuanian servitors, who were still required to serve and who did not enjoy the full rights and privileges of the upper levels of Lithuanian society. As the practice of meeting in local deliberative bodies on the Polish pattern spread, the assertiveness of the middling Lithuanian nobles increased. When called out to fight at the start of the Livonian War in September 1562, large numbers of servitors refused to obey the commands of their leaders, demanding union and the extension to them of the privileges enjoyed by their Polish counterparts. Following the definitive establishment in the 1560s of sejmiki, which largely followed the Polish model, the Second Lithuanian Statute of 1566 formally established a bicameral Sejm on Polish lines; 3 years later the triumph of the middling nobility, in alliance with the Poles, was crowned with the Lublin Union.

There were, however, those left behind, since the very complexity of the Lithuanian system of service made it unclear who, exactly, should be included among the new class of citizens. Sigismund I (1506–48) attempted to reform and better regulate the system of service; in 1528, during the long series of wars against Muscovy, the Lithuanian Sejm fixed the amount of service required from service lands for the next 10 years; in 1529 a list of cavalry servitors was drawn up, including 19,842 men from 13,060 families, of which nearly one-third were provided by magnate families. In the 1550s, under Sigismund August (1548–72), the last of the Jagiellonian dynasty, the massive grand ducal estates were surveyed as the basis for an extensive land reform which, by tying the peasants to the land, created a substantial incentive for servitors to demonstrate their status by performing military service, and in the great muster of 1567, 27,776 cavalrymen turned out; on this occasion under a fifth (4890) were provided by the magnates. For generations, the appearance of an ancestor's name in the muster lists of 1528 and 1567 was seen as a clear proof of noble status; many petty servitors, however, were not able to afford the equipment required, and as the Union with Poland both solidified the definition of what constituted a noble and extended substantial privileges to those who were able to do so, a substantial group of boyars were effectively excluded from the Promised Land of noble privilege. Some sank into the peasantry; others managed to continue their precarious existence in service to great magnate houses.

The Union of Lublin was, however, merely one of the most important stepping-stones in the gradual – though never complete – convergence of the Commonwealth's noble élites. Cultural and political integration continued after 1569, marked by the spread of the Polish language and Catholicism among Lithuanian and Ruthenian nobles. The transfer of Podolia, Volhynia and the Ukrainian lands to the Kingdom of Poland by Sigismund August

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 274
text:
during the bitter discussions at the 1569 Lublin Sejm, in order to put pressure on those Lithuanian magnates opposing the Union, encouraged both the immigration of Polish nobles to these territories, and the increasing involvement of great Ruthenian families in Polish politics. Yet integration had its limits. Local identities remained strong, and sejmiki provided an important focus for local political action. The truncated Grand Duchy of Lithuania which finally accepted the Union retained its own army, administration and law, as well as a powerful sense of autonomy. For all the influence of the middling Lithuanian nobility on the events of 1569, the power of the magnates across the vast lands of the old Grand Duchy in its pre-1569 borders remained much more substantial than in Poland.

In the heartlands of the old Grand Duchy, the transition did not cause substantial social disruption; it was, however, to be a different matter in the Ukrainian lands, where the limits of convergence soon became apparent. Many leading Ruthenian families, including the Vyshnevetsky (Wiśniowiecki), Chartorysky (Czartoryski) and Sangushko (Sanguszko), enthusiastically embraced the ethos of the szlachta in the century after 1569. Their conversion to Catholicism was an important part of a process in which the Commonwealth's noble élites moved away from the religious divisions which had followed the Reformation, when large numbers had turned Protestant, towards an increasing identification of Catholicism as a defining feature of the Commonwealth's ruling élite, a process cemented by the wars of the mid-seventeenth century with Sweden and Muscovy. This left large groups in the Ukrainian lands, who by their lifestyle were little different to the middling and petty nobility of the rest of the Commonwealth, poised awkwardly between its undoubtedly attractive socio-political model and its increasingly unwelcoming cultural and religious exclusivism. The emergence of Cossack society in the second half of the sixteenth century provided an alternative, in which some petty and middling Ruthenian nobles sought the military employment which was such a traditional part of the concept of noble functions. Yet the creation of a large Cossack host, useful to the Commonwealth though it was in time of war, was felt by many to be a potential threat to noble liberties, since the Vasa monarchs Sigismund III (1587–1632), Władysław IV (1632–48) and John Casimir (1648–68) all saw the Cossacks as a potential source of military support for their ambitious political plans to strengthen the monarchy.

For over half a century, the Commonwealth and the Cossacks coexisted in an ill-defined and ambiguous relationship which finally shattered apart in the great Cossack rising of 1648. The 1659 Treaty of Hadiach sought to integrate the Cossack élites into the noble nation by creating a Grand Duchy of Ruthenia and guaranteeing a place in the noble nation to Orthodoxy, but opposition from nobles in the rest of the Commonwealth to the mass ennoblement of Cossacks and the extension of privileges to the Orthodox Church caused its failure. The Cossack revolt and the wars against Muscovy

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 275
text:
(1654–67) and Sweden (1655–60), when the loyalty of Orthodox and Protestant nobles came into question, marked the final triumph of Catholicism, though it was not until 1718 that Protestants were formally excluded from sitting in the Sejm. The Cossack revolt had tested the solidarity of the property-owning nobility in the Ukrainian lands with those elements, so numerous elsewhere in the Commonwealth, who supported themselves by fighting – itself a perfectly respectable noble occupation – but whose religion and way of life could not be accommodated within the political system. The Commonwealth's ethos was in many ways still far more attractive than that of the Muscovite tsar to whom the Cossacks had looked for protection in 1654, and it continued to influence the development of the Cossack hetmanate after 1659, but the noble nation had established its first frontier.

IV

Nevertheless, the szlachta remained extremely diverse. This was inevitable, since it was extremely large. Noble status was conferred upon all children of a noble, both male and female; the szlachta, already large in 1569, therefore had a distinct tendency to grow very quickly. Quite how large it grew is unclear. Connor estimated it to constitute nearly the tenth part of the population at the end of the seventeenth century; from the nineteenth century, the figure of 8–10 per cent was widely accepted. As scholars began to investigate the sources more systematically, however, rather than rely on impressionistic estimates, a more realistic figure emerged. Of particular importance are the registers for the hearth tax raised at various points after 1629, the poll tax levied on four occasions between 1662 and 1676, and the censuses taken at the end of the eighteenth century; in 1790–92 by the Poles, and by the partitioning powers between 1772 and 1827.

Even making allowance for a degree of inaccuracy in the tax registers, which sought to list all members of noble households over the age of ten, but which were administered by a nobility not renowned for its cheerful acceptance of taxation, local studies have consistently revised downwards the percentage of noble inhabitants: the figures of 4.8 per cent for the palatinates of Poznań and Kalisz and 1.66 per cent for the Cracow palatinate in the mid-seventeenth century are significantly lower than previous claims. Emanuel Rostworowski's widely respected estimate for the late eighteenth century suggests a figure of 6–6.5 per cent of a population of approximately 14 million for the whole Commonwealth before the First Partition in 1772, and 7–7.5 per cent of approximately 10 million thereafter. A more accurate general picture will not emerge until more local studies are complete, but it seems that a figure of 6–7.5 per cent of the population is more likely than 10 per cent. Even this reduced figure, however, means that the Commonwealth's nobility constituted a higher percentage of the total population than anywhere else in Europe, with only Spain and Hungary coming close.

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 276
text:
As significant as the size of the nobility was its highly uneven distribution, which reflected the differing histories and traditions of the Commonwealth's component parts. In general, there were fewer nobles in Lithuania and Ukraine – less than 0.5–1 per cent in the palatinates of Kiev and Bratslav – than in Poland, although parts of western Lithuania, especially Samogitia (Żemaitija), also had a high concentration of petty nobles. Even within Poland there were substantial variations, with fewer nobles on the whole in Royal Prussia and Little Poland than in Great Poland. The tendency of the petty szlachta to group together meant that local concentrations could be high, even in Little Poland: although some parishes in the Cracow palatinate had no noble inhabitants, there were 23 where the noble population was over 5 per cent, and four where it was between 8.6 per cent and 12.8 per cent. It was, however, Mazovia which saw the greatest concentration: some estimates put the noble population as high as 20–25 per cent, and villages inhabited entirely by nobles were not uncommon.

No estimate of the size of the nobility can ever be entirely accurate, since it proved impossible in practice to establish a firm boundary between noble and commoner, despite the apparently simple definition of nobility and the control the nobility exercised in theory and at law over its own membership. The number of formal ennoblements did diminish after the king was deprived of his independent initiative in 1578: the Sejm created 334 new nobles, mostly for military service, between 1578 and 1601, and granted Polish nobility (indygenat) to six foreigners. Another 336 native ennoblements and 183 rights of indygenat were granted between 1601 and 1764. According to the Third Lithuanian Statute (1588) Jews converting to Catholicism automatically obtained noble status, although the numbers involved appear to have been small until the 1760s.

There were less formal ways of entering the nobility. In such a vast State, with such a large population of petty nobles, it was not difficult for a commoner, particularly if he had money, to adopt the hallmarks of a noble lifestyle and to pass himself off as noble. Since the bearing of arms had long been regarded as one of the central functions of the nobility, and since there was always a substantial number of commoners in the Commonwealth's armies, it was relatively easy for commoners with long military service to slip into the nobility without formal ennoblement, especially since they often served among petty, landless nobles. But military service was not essential: Many simply adopted a surname of the noble type and moved: Mazovia's numerous population of petty nobles was constantly overspilling into other regions and it was easy to claim noble status in a far-off part of the Commonwealth where it was difficult for checks to be made. Another favourite route was through service to magnates, who felt more able to rely on the loyalty of clients whose status was in some doubt. Money could not only buy villages and estates, which was technically illegal for commoners, but also be used to draw up documents or persuade or bribe witnesses to testify to one's noble

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 277
text:
lineage; indeed it was not uncommon for a would-be noble deliberately to foment an accusation against himself, thereby affording him an opportunity to secure a definitive ruling on his status in court.

The extent of the problem is demonstrated by the notorious Liber generationis plebeanorum, universally known as Liber chamorum, drawn up in manuscript by Walerian Trepka between 1626 and 1639 and only published in full in 1963. A poor noble himself, Trepka was an inveterate gossip. Much of the material he collected was based on hearsay, but he ruthlessly pointed the finger at those he accused of usurping noble status; subsequent research has revealed the accuracy of many of his findings. He made his intentions quite clear in his preface, condemning the increasing frequency with which commoners were styling themselves noble and attempting to enter the nobility. He listed the means by which this was achieved and named names extensively, avidly recounting scandal and salacious detail:

> Borowski: . . . the son of a peasant, an idiot who could neither read nor write; a yokel and a boor; had a peasant wife as well. Bought land.
>
> Fresser, Urban: Cracow burgher. These Fressers only began to pass themselves off as noble in 1626, but we do not want them, because ‘Fresser' (in German) means glutton, and the Polish nobility prefers drinking to eating.
>
> Jasiński, Matyusz: who was deputy starosta of Sieradz for several years . . . He had a nephew, Turski, who frequently said to his face: ‘A peasant and a bastard, who dares boast of his nobility to me!' For he knew he was a peasant. This Turski finally killed him in the street in 1628. It was said that [Turski] slept with [Jasiński's] wife, his own aunt . . . He married his daughter by his first wife to the burgrave of Kalisz.
>
> Jugowicz, . . . was a burgher from Grodzka street in Cracow; his family was from the country, from Myślenice . . . This Oleksy Jugowicz was terribly humpbacked and could not turn his neck. As black as a gypsy, and he pretended he was a nobleman. He traded in salt . . .

Such entries are typical. Trepka was only too ready to challenge individuals in the courts and was not afraid to accuse great families of conniving in the acquisition of nobility by commoners, listing 64 such cases involving the Lubomirski family alone.

Whether or not Trepka's work is entirely accurate, it reflects extensive contemporary concern at the ease with which commoners could pass themselves off as noble and gives some indication of how widespread the phenomenon was: the Liber chamorum essentially covered western Little Poland – although Trepka did make occasional forays further afield – and his own lifetime (he died in 1640), but it lists 2537 individuals – about

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 278
text:
three times the number ennobled by the Sejm for the entire Commonwealth between 1578 and 1764. Thus in practice, it could be relatively easy for a wealthy urban patrician to pass by one route or another into the nobility if he so desired, as did 26 (23.6 per cent) of 110 members of Cracow city council in the seventeenth century. For burghers of the great cities, the line between noble and commoner was already somewhat blurred. Cracow possessed noble status under a 1493 charter, confirmed in 1513, which permitted it as a corporate entity to own land; similar rights were extended to Wilno in 1568 and Lwów in 1658. Poznań, in Great Poland, and the Prussian cities of Danzig, Thorn and Elbing also possessed this privilege. Cracow, Danzig, Elbing, Lublin, Lwów, Poznań, Thorn and Wilno had the right to participate in royal elections; in 1632, the representatives of Danzig and Thorn made a point by claiming, albeit unsuccessfully, the right to vote separate from, and before, the Royal Prussian nobility. In these circumstances, it was relatively easy for burghers to acquire land: in Danzig in the fifteenth century, only 11 out of 132 members of the council (8.5 per cent) owned land, but by the seventeenth century, exactly half (31 out of 62) did so. From owning land to joining the nobility could be but a short step.

Thus Trepka's complaints were ineffectual: the Commonwealth's nobility remained open for many who wished to join it without the formality of an act of the Sejm. The succession of statutes attempting to seal off the nobility and define it more closely bears eloquent testimony to the ease with which they were circumvented. The ineffectiveness of the 1496 ban on commoners buying or leasing land is demonstrated by its renewal in 1538 and 1611, to similarly little effect, while an act of 1717 reflected continuing concern by attempting to ban the foundation of new towns or villages by those of uncertain status. An act of 1633 sought to deprive nobles resident in towns of their status if they took municipal office: the result was that, initially at least, burghers entering the nobility resigned from their town councils. Later in the century, the law was often ignored: Dominik Meglioruci, elected to the Cracow council in June 1697, was ennobled by the Sejm in September of the same year, yet served on the council until at least 1722. Frustration at the complete inability of the law to prevent the usurpation of noble status brought a revival of the medieval concept of scartabelat: a cadet nobility which did not enjoy full noble privileges. In the election charter of Michael Korybut Wiśniowiecki (1669–73), this idea was enshrined in a clause which banned anyone from holding public office until their family had enjoyed noble status for three generations. Challenges to those suspected of usurping noble status remained common into the eighteenth century, but in practice this law, like so many others, was frequently ignored. Indeed, there is evidence to suggest that insulting a fellow nobleman by calling his status into question could backfire on the perpetrator: at the second Sejm of 1654, when a dispute erupted between two members of the Chamber of Envoys, one Borysyło, deputy cupbearer of Kiev, and a certain Korzewski, deputy judge
