label: p. 279
text:
of Nowogródek, Borysyło accused Korzewski of being a peasant, and therefore unable to take up his seat. The shocked Korzewski reacted angrily and both men were asked to leave the room. The other envoys, who had been greatly disturbed by the incident, objected to Borysyło's tone, however, and preferred to accept the view of Korzewski's local sejmik, which had elected him; he was therefore allowed to take up his seat.

V

Nobility might, therefore, be relatively easy to acquire for those who desired it and who had acquired some, at least, of the trappings of nobility. Maintaining an economic position sufficient to support a noble lifestyle without recourse to plebeian pursuits was far more difficult. The nobility might be equal before the law, but it varied widely in its economic condition, from a tiny group at the top, which controlled vast estates to the landless gołota (the naked ones) at the bottom. The fact that the nobility paid extraordinary taxes voted by the Sejm makes it possible, where records have survived, to document this economic diversity. The act introducing the poll tax in 1662 divided the nobility into various groups. Possessores or posesjonaci – noble landholders in possession of allodial or leasehold estates – were to pay 3 zloties, and 1.5 for their wives and children above the age of ten. Impossessionati – nobles without land who earned their living through military service, or service at the Court or on the estate of a rich noble – were to pay 2 zloties. A noble landholder without serfs who worked his own land up to a fixed amount (about 16 hectares), paid 2 zloties for himself and 15 groszy for his wife and children. Poorer nobles – the szlachta częstkowa, who owned or leased part of a village, and the szlachta zagrodowa (smallholders) – each paid 1 zloty, and 15 groszy for their wives and children. In the palatinate of Cracow in 1662, just over half of the nobility (2275 out of 4279) were classified as possessores; 485 (11.5 per cent) were listed as impossessionati; 227 (5.3 per cent) served other nobles as estate factors or managers; 788 (18.4 per cent) served in a more humble capacity; 405 (9.5 per cent) were classified as smallholders and 99 (2.3 per cent) represented the poor nobility who farmed their land themselves. The 1673 act renewing the poll tax divided the nobility into noble landholders (szlachta osiadła), nobles in service, and nobles without serfs. In the palatinates of Poznań and Kalisz, 5133 out of 9484 nobles came into the first category (54.1 per cent), 484 were classed as factors or estate managers (5.1 per cent), 3029 (32 per cent) as nobles in service, 361 (3.8 per cent) as poor nobles – mostly szlachta częstkowa – and 477 (5 per cent) as smallholders without serfs.

Even in the Polish heartlands, therefore, only just over half the nobility was classed as independent, resident landholders. In Podlasie and parts of the palatinate of Lublin, but above all in Mazovia, the poor nobility was dominant: noble smallholders (szlachta zagrodowa) held 23.4 łan

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 280
text:
(1 łan = approximately 40 acres) of land per square mile in sixteenth-century Mazovia, compared with two for Great Poland and 1.3 in Little Poland. In some areas, it was substantially higher: 89.6 per cent of the land was already held by noble smallholders by the end of the sixteenth century in the district of Nur, 79.5 per cent in the district of Wizna and 78.7 per cent in the district of Łomża. Mazovia was exceptional, but in the Commonwealth as a whole it is estimated that by the end of the eighteenth century some 125,000 nobles (16.7 per cent) were comfortably off (bene possessionati); there were some 300,000 lesser-noble property-holders (40 per cent), 150,000 who rented their property (20 per cent) and 175,000 in service and various professions (23.3 per cent).

The large number of noble smallholders and poor nobles was encouraged by the laws and customs surrounding the inheritance of land. The effects of partible inheritance were exacerbated by the protection afforded by law to the property rights of noblewomen. Normally, a quarter of an estate was allocated to any daughters to provide them with dowries, the rest was divided up amongst the sons. Often shares were allocated by the father to sons as they came of age, subject to guarantees designed to protect widows in respect of the property they had brought to the couple as dowry. Partible inheritance tended rapidly to reduce the family patrimony and income; by the late sixteenth century perhaps the majority of the Commonwealth's nobility was poor or at least impoverished. The economic condition of many was often worse than that of peasants, and was frequently commented on by foreigners: in the 1670s, Ulrich Werdum, from Frisia, expressed his surprise at seeing a Mazovian nobleman proudly wearing his sabre as he drove manure to his field himself. Surplus children were sent to serve richer nobles, or rented tiny plots of land from larger landowners, or took up a military career, or migrated to the towns, where they swelled the ranks of the indigent szlachta brukowa, the ‘pavement nobility', or dropped out of the nobility altogether.

The relative impoverishment of so many and the constant threat of poverty for a great many more ensured that many of the theoretical constraints upon the economic activities permitted to nobles were, in practice, ignored. At the end of the sixteenth century, the English traveller Fynes Moryson observed:

> In generali, a gentelman will not marry a marchants daughter, nor any ignoble woman, for any riches whatsoever, and if any should so marry, his Kinsmen would force him to be divorced, for they are so carefull not to stayne their nobility, insomuch as a gentleman will not buy or sell anything, but his owne come and catle.

A hundred years later, Connor noted that ‘they never intermarry with the Common People' when he discussed the concept of nobility in Poland, but

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 281
text:
later, in describing how nobility was acquired, testified that practice was very different from theory. Noble status was conferred:

> first by birth, where both the Parents were Noble: Nevertheless, now-a-days, by a long Tract of Custom, not only such are reputed Noble, but likewise those whose Mothers were Plebeians, for nothing is at present more practis'd in Poland than for the Gentry to match with the Commonality, especially with those that are rich.

Connor's instinct was right: the practice of mésalliance had continued unchecked throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Many nobles, particularly poor nobles with daughters, were only too willing to marry their children off to burghers or even peasants, without any feeling that they were compromising their noble status. No doubt Trepka was spinning in his grave.

Commercial activity was another means of trying to guarantee the sort of income necessary to keep up noble appearances. The richer nobles were extensively involved in trade, commerce, manufacturing and money-lending (albeit usually through the medium of factors and managers), and lesser nobles were quite prepared to move to towns or cities in pursuit of a livelihood. Many urban nobles were happy to engage in commercial activities, and the phenomenon of the noble artisan was by no means unknown. The town of Bochnia in the Cracow palatinate, which had grown rich on the proceeds from its salt-mines, provides a good example both of the way in which rich burghers were able to pass into the ranks of the nobility, and of the extent to which nobles migrated to towns to engage in activities which theoretically threatened them with derogation, while still maintaining their noble status. Between 1531 and 1630, about 30 per cent of patrician families in Bochnia used the title nobilis. Between 1535 and 1642, 40 nobles acquired citizenship in Bochnia, which was also held by a further six. Some of these were already wealthy, such as Mikołaj Stadnicki, the inheritor of one town and 25 villages, who settled in Bochnia at the end of the sixteenth century; others were quite content to grow rich on the proceeds of the salt trade, or even the artisanal activities which fed upon it, without feeling it compromised their noble status. Involvement in such supposedly derogating activities certainly did not prevent these urban nobles from participating in the general political life of the palatinate or the Commonwealth: several had close links with the royal Court, and one family – the Wielopolskis – rose out of the Bochnia patriciate in the seventeenth century to a place among the Commonwealth's magnate élite.

VI

The seething ant heap of poor and impoverished nobles contrasted vividly with the tiny élite of wealthy families at the apex of the social system.

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 282
text:
Between the late sixteenth and the early eighteenth century several factors increased the gap between a small number of rich nobles and the ordinary szlachta. Economic developments played a part in this process. Richer nobles profited most from the favourable market conditions of the sixteenth century, while the impact of the long series of wars fought within the Commonwealth's borders after 1648 merely intensified this trend: poorer nobles lost a significant part of their land to wealthier landowners, who were better able through their economic and political power to avoid or absorb the worst effects of the wars and the downturn in demand for Polish grain. On the whole, those owning several villages increased their holdings, those owning one or two managed to hold their own, while it was the poor nobility which did worst. One study of the Kalisz district in Great Poland shows that between 1580 and 1655 the number of villages held by those owning only part of a village dropped dramatically, from 160 to 92, which was from 51 per cent of the villages in the district to 29 per cent. Those holding more than two villages increased their holdings from 50 villages (16 per cent) to 96 (30 per cent).

Access to royal land often played a vital part in this process. Royal estates comprised some 15–20 per cent of the Commonwealth's land, but the king was in no position to administer the royal domain directly and individual estates – known as starosties (starostwa) – were leased out, in most cases for life. Since few officials enjoyed a salary, the grant of a starosty was in theory a reward for public service; in practice, the proceeds far outweighed any service rendered. This was despite the triumph in the 1560s of the anti-aristocratic ‘Movement for the Execution of the Laws', which sought to prevent the alienation of the royal domain and put royal finances on a firm footing. Henceforth, in theory, the kwarta – one-quarter of net, one-fifth of gross revenue from royal lands – was assigned to the upkeep of the small army which protected the south-eastern frontier. The noble leaseholder was to keep a further fifth, with the rest returning to the royal – from 1590 the state – treasury. The monarchy's inability to carry out regular audits of its estates or to enforce the law, however, soon ensured that although payment of the kwarta was fairly regular from the early seventeenth century, in practice the leaseholder kept the rest of the proceeds. Ironically, the triumph of the Execution Movement had the opposite effect to the one intended; moreover, the limited reforms that were introduced did not apply to Lithuania.

Starosties varied widely in profitability, but they contributed significantly to the economic well-being of their holders. Some, particularly in the east, were highly lucrative. The starosty of Bila Tserkva near Kiev, the richest in the whole Commonwealth, was valued for the kwarta in 1771 at 63,506 zloties, an enormous sum; altogether there were six starosties in the Kiev palatinate alone valued at over 10,000 zloties. The select few who acquired several starosties could reap substantial profits. The royal land held by some

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 283
text:
was equal to or greater than their inherited properties; and it was in great part due to the proceeds from royal land that magnates were able to build up their private holdings. Almost half of the grain produced on the estates of Aleksander Michał Lubomirski in 1660 came from lands leased from the Crown. Janusz Ostrogski, holder of the vast Ostrogski entail, held at his death in 1620 over 1127 villages, of which over half belonged to the Crown. The bloated private latifundia of the greatest magnates were thus built up at the expense of the royal and the State treasury.

These great complexes of land, frequently scattered across a wide area, gave their owners the important advantage of flexibility. Concentration on the European economy has tended to exaggerate the importance of the Baltic grain market and play down the significance of the internal market: only some 2.5 per cent of the grain produced in the Commonwealth was exported, even during the boom years of the sixteenth century, and sales on the internal market were worth four to five times more. Far from being dependent merely upon the Baltic trade, magnates were well placed to exploit all kinds of markets, both internal and external, and to sell not just grain, but timber, livestock, and a wide variety of raw materials; indeed the Ukrainian lands, where many of the largest latifundia were based, being far from the river network which served the Baltic, concentrated more on the lucrative cattle trade.

The agrarian economy was more varied than is often appreciated. While serfdom was certainly important, it was by no means the uniform system as which it is often portrayed, however convenient that view might be for general theories about the development of the European economy. The extent of labour-service (robot) obligations varied widely; in some areas, such as Royal Prussia, estates were almost entirely worked by hired labour. Even where serfdom was common, there was extensive use of hired labour: most large estates could not function without it, particularly at harvest-time. In Great Poland 10–15 per cent of the peasantry was free, working as hired labour for noble estates on contracts; 91 per cent of 337 estates studied in Little Poland between 1512 and 1642 used hired labour. Even on manorial estates based on robot, the demesne constituted only about 25 per cent of the land; the remaining 75 per cent was made up of peasant plots, which were far from subsistence farms, but were often heavily involved in the local market; 50 per cent of peasant farms in Little Poland in 1590 were themselves employers of hired labour.

Large estates based on serf labour undoubtedly enjoyed certain advantages. Those with access to the great river network could undercut smaller producers because their transport costs were lower since they eliminated middlemen by using their own flotillas of barges. When the relative profitability of the Danzig trade declined from about the mid-seventeenth century, large landowners were well placed to find alternative sources of income. On the Zamoyski entail in the second half of the eighteenth century,

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 284
text:
income from the Danzig trade fluctuated from 7.6–21.6 per cent of overall revenue between 1767 and 1781; on average it was 11.6 per cent. The greater part of the entail's income came from rent, which constituted on average 34.2 per cent of income between 1767 and 1798 and the propinacja – the exploitation of the nobility's practical monopoly of the production and sale of alcohol – which produced an average 29.9 per cent of income between 1767 and 1798. The propinacja, in which landlords made huge profits by selling alcohol to their own peasants, was merely one example of the way in which they sought to maximize income through a kind of mercantilist policy designed to exploit the serf-based system. By the eighteenth century, many estates were involved in manufacturing enterprises of various kinds – particularly glass and textiles – not merely the production of alcohol, and the estate's peasants were frequently (if not always effectively) forbidden to buy certain products except from their overlord. These enterprises were designed to capitalize on the raw materials in such abundant supply on the great latifundia, but the practical problems, not least of transport, meant that the vast majority, apart from the breweries and distilleries, were short-lived.

In the favourable political and economic conditions down to the mid-seventeenth century, the foundations of the staggering fortunes of such as the Radziwiłłs – one of the richest noble families in Europe – the Sieniawskis or the Zasławskis were laid. It is difficult, however, to establish just how profitable these latifundia were. Estimates of magnate income by dumbstruck foreign observers, or even by nobles themselves, should be taken with a certain degree of scepticism. It has been estimated that Janusz Ostrogski's annual income from his vast estates probably did not exceed 400,000 zloties in the early seventeenth century, about double that of Jan Zamoyski. Nevertheless, a tiny group was certainly able to lead lives of great splendour, and their courts were major centres of patronage and employment for many impoverished nobles. Stanisław Lubomirski (1583–1649) maintained a permanent court of some 270 people, excluding menial servants. Many magnates kept private military retinues, as much for display as for defence, but they could mobilize large numbers in an emergency. Lubomirski himself maintained some 600 men which, with uniforms and arms, must have cost him something like 108,000 zloties per year. Tomasz Zamoyski brought 1700 to the 1632 royal election, while that of 1669 drew substantial contingents: Private wars between these forces were not uncommon.

These men were wealthy and cosmopolitan aristocrats well able to dazzle their European contemporaries. When they travelled abroad they made a particular effort to impress: the entrance of Jerzy Ossoliński to Rome in 1633 caused a sensation, accompanied as he was by 300 retainers in Polish costume, 30 mules in scarlet, ten camels in gilded silk, a personal guard of 30 cavalrymen and six splendid Turkish horses trotting on gold horseshoes. Travel certainly broadened the mind: the courts of these magnates gave ample testimony to the sophisticated influences picked up abroad. Jan

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 285
text:
Zamoyski built an entire Renaissance city at Zamość, complete with university and fortifications constructed according to the latest designs. Stanisław Lubomirski had a private chapel with an orchestra of fifteen and a choir of three castrati, three altos, three tenors and five bases; Władysław Dominik Zasławski's musicians cost some 12,000 zloties per annum. The 150-odd waggons taken by the Swedes from the looted Lubomirski castle of Wiśnicz in 1655 contained works of art by Raphael, Titian and Veronese, among many others; in the eighteenth century, Wincenty Potocki's collection of engravings and drawings was reputed to contain 3500 items by Rubens alone.

VII

Wealth brought power. From the late sixteenth century, the influence of a small number of families within the political system grew enormously. The limiting after 1569 of the monarchy's financial independence meant that the royal Court was in an almost constant state of penury and could not act as the centre of social life in the way it did elsewhere in Europe. Chronic suspicion of royal intentions prevented the emergence of a substantial military establishment, and the inability of the inadequate fiscal system to pay the Commonwealth's forces during the long cycle of defensive wars between 1648 and 1721 meant that the royal government was wholly unable to provide careers compatible with noble ideas of suitable employment which impoverished nobles might have welcomed and which the developing military and administrative systems of the Commonwealth's neighbours had begun to provide: by the mid-eighteenth century, a substantial number of nobles from Great Poland were serving in the Prussian army.

Wealthy nobles partly filled this gap. It was on their estates, at their courts and in their private military retinues that poorer nobles sought employment as factors, administrators or servants. Others leased or rented lands from magnates who could not or would not farm all their lands directly, especially in the second half of the seventeenth century, when the depredations of war stimulated the widespread development of the szlachta czynszowa: landless nobles who rented their properties. In consequence, magnates commanded significant clientèles made up of nobles who depended on them directly or indirectly for their livelihood. The Commonwealth's political structure gave these clientèles great scope: the liberum veto – the extension of the principle of unanimity in debate which enabled one envoy to break the proceedings of a Sejm or sejmik, first recognized in 1652 – enabled faction leaders to block the policies of their rivals, while the fact that envoys to the Sejm were delegates from their sejmiki, furnished with instructions, not representatives with plenipotentiary powers, meant that magnates were able to use their local power bases to win significant leverage at the centre of politics. Connor was amused that a noble servant might be beaten frequently by his master for his misdemeanours, yet still have as good a vote in the Sejm;

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 286
text:
it was unlikely, however, that he would speak in other than his master's voice.

The great economic and political power of this small élite thus undermined in practice the theoretical equality of the szlachta. Although attempts to introduce a hierarchy of titles had long been resisted and royal attempts to introduce orders of chivalry, such as Władysław IV's ill-fated Order of the Immaculate Conception, were condemned as assaults on the principle of noble equality, this did not prevent a number of families using them. Lithuanian and Ruthenian families descended from the houses of Rurik or Gedymin were legally allowed to use the title of prince (kniaz in Ruthenian, książę in Polish). Foreign nobles continued to use their titles if they obtained Polish nobility; native nobles were all too keen to seek honours abroad: the Radziwiłłs, Lubomirskis and Ossolińskis were dukes of the Holy Roman Empire and the Myszkowskis were created marquises of the Empire by Pope Clement VIII. Several families became counts or barons of the Empire, including the Tarnowskis, the Leszczyńskis, the Chodkiewicz and the Tęczyńskis; Paprocki printed their patents of nobility in his armorial. Although there was a great uproar at the temerity of Urban VIII, who created a duchy in Poland for Jerzy Ossoliński in 1633, many families linked their imperial titles with their Polish lands, using titles such as comes in Tarnow or comes in Wisnicz. Although it was occasionally prudent not to flaunt titles in public, in private they were invariably used.

Titles were, however, of relatively minor significance. Differences in status within the nobility, which elsewhere were denoted by a hierarchy of titles, were in the Commonwealth provided by the hierarchy of office. At its head was the Senate, ranked according to a strict order of precedence led by the two Catholic archbishops (of Gniezno and Lwów) and fifteen Catholic bishops. The leading lay senator was the castellan of Cracow, ahead of the palatines, among whom were counted the castellans of Wilno and Troki and the starosta general of Samogitia. Next came the major castellans, who were governors of the royal castle in the leading city of each palatinate, then the minor castellans, governors of royal castles in lesser cities, of whom there were none in Lithuania. Technically ranked at the bottom of the Senate, though actually possessing the enormous prestige of power, were ten government ministers: the grand marshals, chancellors, vice-chancellors, treasurers and marshals of the Court, of whom there was one each for Poland and Lithuania.

Certain non-senatorial offices were also highly prized, particularly the posts of grand or field hetman (commanders of the Polish and Lithuanian armies), which conferred a great deal of power, and of court treasurer, which was lucrative, as well as a number of honorific posts, such as chamberlain, steward, or carver, whose duties, if they existed, were largely ceremonial; these dignities were, nevertheless, much coveted: they were frequently the preserve of young members of prominent families. For lesser families, there

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795

text:
was a network of local offices, military, judicial and honorific. Of these few had any real responsibilities; nevertheless, to be swordbearer of Cracow, cupbearer of Sandomierz or ensign of Mścisław was of great local significance. Individuals were invariably known by the offices that they held, and there was as definite a hierarchy of prestige with regard to local offices as in the Senate.

Thus for all its egalitarianism the szlachta was as status-conscious as any of its European counterparts. If nobles of whatever rank were addressed as pan brat (literally 'sir brother') and commoners as 'przyjaciół' (friend), senators were referred to as 'elder brethren', and the Latin term 'procer' was freely used to denote individuals at the summit of the social pyramid. In personal correspondence there were strict rules: wielmożny (roughly the Polish equivalent of procer) denoted a senator, urodzony (high-born) was used to other office-holders, and szlachetny (noble) to non office-holders. By the late seventeenth century, titular inflation had set in: wielmożny was used liberally for any office-holder, while urodzony frequently denoted a noble property-owner. Concern with status led to a veritable mania for titles, as sons of a palatine (wojewoda) would call themselves wojewodzic, sons of a castellan would be addressed as kasztelanic and the children of lesser office-holders claimed a series of bizarre appellations. By the early eighteenth century, many of the old taboos were increasingly ignored: if the Order of the Immaculate Conception collapsed in 1638 amid bitter protest from the middle and petty nobility, Augustus II (1697–1733) freely distributed his Order of the White Eagle, instituted in 1705, despite the continuing legal ban on such baubles.

VIII

It might seem, therefore, that a small group of wealthy families had subverted the egalitarianism which still formally survived, and stealthily overturned the victories won by the mass of the nobility in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Historians in the Polish Peoples Republic after 1945, required to write within a broadly Marxist framework, devoted much attention to documenting and explaining this phenomenon. From the 1950s, the standard interpretation of the Commonwealth's development was that the sixteenth-century ‘szlachta democracy' was overturned by a ‘magnate oligarchy' during the seventeenth century. As the power of these magnates grew, they seized control of the helm of state in their own ‘reactionary' interests, while pretending to keep up the façade of the ‘progressive' szlachta democracy which they consistently undermined.

This theory was thought to provide a model of Polish development which might explain its divergence from the general European pattern. There are, however, serious objections to it. First, the classic period of the ‘magnate oligarchy', which was meant to have started at some point after 1648, corresponded exactly with the period in which the Commonwealth's political

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 288
text:
system decayed into apparent anarchy. If the magnates did seize control of the ‘helm of state' to rule in their own interests, why did this powerful oligarchy allow the collapse of central government? Second, it proved remarkably difficult to agree on the attributes of a magnate. It is impossible to define any élite group on the basis purely of landholding, since the value of property varied greatly from one part of the Commonwealth to another: Dworzaczek calculated that a nobleman from Little Poland would have to own twenty villages to enjoy the same income as his counterpart from Great Poland who merely owned ten. Senate membership was important, but the Senate was small – only 150-strong at its peak in the seventeenth century, of which 52 were minor castellans of lesser prestige – and the practice of life-tenure of office meant that turnover was slow. Many members of wealthy and powerful families were therefore not senators or dignitaries; indeed many senators, particularly the minor castellans, were of comparatively humble backgrounds. Other attributes were therefore suggested as vital to the categorization of this élite, including birth, connections, lifestyle, education and standing amongst the local szlachta, but are too subjective and imprecise to be particularly helpful.

The problem with attempts to delineate a magnate élite is that they assume a stability at the top level of noble society which did not exist. Although social life and politics were dominated in particular periods by a tiny élite of families and individuals, this élite was subject to constant change, with only a handful of families maintaining their position unchallenged. There is a natural tendency within any aristocracy for families to rise, decline or die out, but certain peculiar features of the Commonwealth's political and social structure ensured that the instability within its élite was greater than elsewhere in Europe and does much to explain why noble society in the Commonwealth failed to settle down into the stability and relative calm experienced in other noble-dominated societies between the mid-seventeenth century and the French Revolution.

No family could take its position for granted. Office may have performed a roughly similar function to titles in other nobilities with regard to the delineation of status, but its possession was more significant than that: it helped maintain influence at local level, while the importance to the monarchy of Senate support ensured that senators increasingly monopolized leases on royal land: the percentage of starosties in the hands of Polish senators and central dignitaries between 1697 and 1763 varied from palatinate to palatinate, but nowhere was it lower than 56 per cent (palatinate of Sieradz) and the highest figure was in the Rawa palatinate, where it reached 99 per cent. Out of 22 palatinates in the kingdom of Poland, in nine the figure was between 90 and 99 per cent; in five it was between 80 and 89 per cent, in six it was between 70 and 79 per cent; only in the palatinates of Sieradz and Podlasie (62 per cent) was it under 70 per cent. And 79 per cent of government ministers, 43 per cent of palatines and 30 per cent of central dignitaries held starosties valued at over 10,000 zloties in 1771.

Office, however, was not automatically passed on from father to son, and the most important were in such demand that attainment of senatorial rank by an individual did not guarantee that his relatives or children

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 289
text:
would, even though families are often categorized as 'senatorial' on the basis of a couple of appointments: the Tarłos, eight of whom were palatines of Lublin between 1574 and 1744, were the exception rather than the rule. No other family came close to the Radziwiłłs, who provided twelve palatines of Wilno between 1491 and 1795, seven Lithuanian grand chancellors, one vice-chancellor, four grand marshals, six grand hetmans, two field hetmans, three castellans of Wilno, and a cardinal, as well as filling a large number of more minor offices. The Radziwiłłs, however, were unique: the fact that they held three of the six entails designated by the Sejm in the late sixteenth century meant that they had an economic base whose security was matched by no other family in the Commonwealth.

The king, who appointed senators and central dignitaries, remained the most important factor in the scramble for office. All monarchs were, in practice, able to promote a substantial number of new figures to important offices, and were capable of blocking members of well-established dynasties. Between 1648 and 1696, 81 of the most coveted posts in Poland (the twenty leading central dignitaries and the Senate, excluding bishops and minor castellans) were filled by 330 men from 186 families. And 59 families had at least two representatives, which means that nearly two-thirds of families only produced one senator in this period. The Potockis had eleven, the Leszczyńskis nine, the Denhoffs, Lubomirskis and Opalińskis eight each, the Koniecpolskis had seven, the Działłyńskis, Grudzińskis and Zamoyskis had six; eleven more families had between three and five. Of 135 senators and dignitaries named by John Casimir from 98 families, 39 were the first members of their families so honoured, which represented 28.9 per cent of the men, and 39.8 per cent of the families appointed. Wiśniowiecki's reign was too short to be of great significance, but seven of his fourteen nominations were new men. John III Sobieski (1674–96) appointed 107 from 82 families; 33 were new men (30.8 per cent of the appointments; 40.2 per cent of the families).

Appointment to high office did not in itself establish an individual's position (still less that of his family) among the élite. With almost a third on average of such appointments being new men, it is difficult to argue that a magnate oligarchy was closing its ranks in the second half of the seventeenth century. Zielińska's study of these offices in the Saxon period (minus three palatines and three castellans of lands lost by 1697) shows that this trend continued: only 30 of 190 families had more than a couple of representatives. Augustus II named 174 men from 112 families, of which 33 per cent were new men, representing 45 families (41 per cent); Augustus III (1733–64) named 57 new men (40 per cent) from 46 families (47 per cent). If there was some closing-up at the top end of the Senate – thirteen men who began their career by appointments to local office between 1648 and 1696 ended up as

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 290
text:
ministers, something which was rare thereafter – nevertheless, it is hard to escape the conclusion that the Commonwealth's political élite was far from a closed, stable oligarchy.

Families could fall as well as rise. John Casimir may have nominated representatives of families with a Senate tradition dating back to the fifteenth or sixteenth century like the Myszkowskis, Opalińskis, Firlejs or Koniecpolskis, but few of them were appointed to particularly prestigious posts; in general, families which had been prominent in the sixteenth century such as the Firlejs, Ostrorógs, Tarnowskis and Zebrzydowskis died out or were eclipsed by relative newcomers like the Lubomirskis, Potockis and Zamoyskis. It was similar in the eighteenth century: some old families including the Leszczyńskis, Koniecpolskis and Sieniawskis died out, to be replaced by new families or families such as the Czartoryskis, which had experienced a hiatus in their office-holding career. Even the Radziwiłłs suffered something of a decline: with one or two exceptions, its members had to content themselves with less prestigious posts than hitherto.

By its very nature, the system caused frequent and bitter frustration and was liable to intense periods of volatility. Since appointment was for life, a monarch had to accept the senators and even ministers bequeathed to him by his predecessor. From the king's point of view, this was highly unsatisfactory; a shortage of convenient deaths could leave him unable to utilize his main political weapon: in 1711 Augustus II only had the opportunity to make one appointment. Coveted offices and starosties were often tied up for years in the hands of individuals: Albrycht Stanisław Radziwiłł, who was appointed Lithuanian Grand Chancellor in 1623 by Sigismund III, died in 1656, having outlived Sigismund's eldest son, Władysław IV. These bottlenecks caused intense frustration: individuals might languish in a relatively unprestigious post for years waiting for advancement. Nevertheless, problems also resulted from the occasional periods of intense upheaval. The early years of John Casimir's reign, which were stormy enough following the outbreak of the 1648 Cossack revolt, saw a period of dramatic change as 26 of the 79 most important Polish seats in the Senate fell vacant in 1649–50; in all, between 1649 and 1652, 47 per cent of Polish offices in the Senate changed hands. John Casimir therefore had an unprecedented opportunity to use his patronage powers, but the results were highly controversial. Krzysztof Opaliński was created palatine of Poznań, one of the most prestigious lay senators, but he had wanted to be Chancellor, and withdrew to his estates in the highest of dudgeon to foment opposition. John Casimir left the office of Polish Grand Hetman vacant for 3 years after 1651, and tried to avoid appointing his enemy, Janusz Radziwiłł, to the grand hetmanship of Lithuania in 1654. Both these cases drew bitter criticism, not only from the disappointed contenders, as did the practice of selling important offices to the highest bidder.

The most volatile periods came in the early eighteenth century, however, during the brief reigns of Stanisław Leszczyński (1704–10 and 1733–36).

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 291
text:
Leszczyński was elected by supporters of Charles XII of Sweden in 1704 during the Great Northern War; following the treaty of Altranstädt (1706), in which Charles forced Augustus II to abdicate, Leszczyński's supporters planned a clean sweep of the major offices of state. Although such decisions were more dependent upon Charles than Leszczyński and although – thanks to the backing of Peter the Great – Augustus's fortunes revived after the Battle of Poltava in 1709, the implications were clear: if Leszczyński won, his opponents faced being stripped of office and royal lands, as John Casimir had done to Polish Vice Chancellor Hieronim Radziejowski in 1652 and Polish Grand Marshal Jerzy Sebastian Lubomirski in 1664 by having them impeached before the Sejm. Similar fears were aroused during the War of the Polish Succession (1733–35) when Leszczyński was the French-backed candidate against Augustus III (1733–64) in a contested election, but he failed once more to consolidate the throne; his supporters understandably did not prosper under Augustus.

Instability also had economic roots. A great deal of study has been devoted to the dazzling fortunes of great nobles, and the ways in which one was accumulated; far less to the problems of preventing its dissipation. Yet partible inheritance was not just a problem for Mazovian smallholders; it also affected the greatest families. In 1586 the sons of Mikołaj Radziwiłł the Black established three separate entails from his vast estates, an example that was followed by the Zamoyskis (1589), Myszkowskis (1601), Ostrogskis (1609) and Sułkowskis (1783). Other families, however, showed no interest in following suit. There was some opposition on the grounds that entails violated the principle of noble equality, but in each of the above cases, Sejm approval was forthcoming in return for the acceptance of certain obligations on the part of the holder. The main reason why only seven were ever established seems to have been lack of interest rather than szlachta opposition. The holder of an entail was not as free to dispose of his property as other landowners: if he had acquired no great allodial holdings outside the entail it was difficult to provide for his younger children, and he could not sell land to pay his creditors, a dilemma that spectacularly confronted Janusz Sanguszko, holder of the ill-fated Ostrogski entail, in 1753.

This lack of flexibility meant that entails were not well suited to the condition of landholding in sparsely populated Eastern Europe, where land was plentiful but of little use without labour to work it; therefore, despite the frequent attempts to compute the area of land held by individual nobles, it is a meaningless exercise: acreage was less important than the number of villages controlled. Rich nobles tended not to own consolidated blocks of land, but a series of estates (folwarki), often scattered in groups round a key estate (klucz), across an enormous area. These holdings were impossible to rationalize, and grouping them in an entail did nothing to create a coherent economic entity, although protection from subdivision did perhaps provide enough stability to encourage the settlement which would bring greater

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 292
text:
profit: the Zamoyski entail grew from 149 villages and six towns in 1605 to 221 villages and ten towns by the end of the eighteenth century, increasing the number of estates from 42 to 97.

Most families were not so protected. The constant division of property to provide children with their share of the family holdings meant that little attention was given to the consolidation of blocks of land, and contiguous estates – even parts of the same village – acquired at different times often continued to be administered separately. Partible inheritance made a great deal of sense: no landowner who held more than one or two villages could hope to administer his lands as a rational block; even in the entails much of the land was not administered directly. Division between sons and daughters of wealthy landowners therefore did not necessarily affect the viability of individual estates or groups of estates: it may even have enhanced it. It did, however, make it difficult for children to sustain the standard of living achieved by their parents.

Even the wealthiest faced enormous problems. Much is often made of the maintenance of 'private armies' by magnates, especially in the light of the State's lack of a large standing army: the existence of these forces is taken to demonstrate the weakness of central power and the increasingly dominant position of the great magnates; after 1945, Polish historians were quick to claim that the large private forces of magnates were part of the structure of feudal oppression. The term 'private army' is, however, at best unhelpful and at worst downright misleading. While it is true that one or two of the wealthiest Lithuanian and Ukrainian magnates did maintain small garrisons organised and equipped on western lines – such as the Radziwiłł garrison at Słuck – the forces that could be raised by what was always the tiniest of minorities even among the aristocracy were far from being professional, modern armies, and they were certainly not standing forces on any scale. Historians have been too quick to accept impressionistic estimates of numbers and the hearsay evidence of diaries, in the absence of detailed muster rolls; where these do exist, the numbers of such private forces come tumbling down. It is true that, on particular occasions, such as royal elections, a handful of magnates could and did show up with impressive retinues. It is claimed that there were 60,000 private troops at the 1632 election of Władysław IV: 10,000 with Krzysztof II Radziwiłł, and 6000 each with Stanisław Konopczynski and one of the Leszczyńskis. Similar numbers are claimed for the 1669 election of Michael Korybut Wiśniowiecki, with Bogusław and Michał Kazimierz Radziwiłł bringing nearly 8000 men, as did Krzysztof and Michał Kazimierz Pac, while Jan Sobieski and Dymitr Wiśniowiecki brought 4000 each. Yet such figures are barely credible, and no magnate, however wealthy, was capable of maintaining forces of anything like this size. Certain magnates, such as the Radziwiłł, could indeed call up substantial numbers of men for particular events such as a royal election, not least because, since the 1560s, the Radziwiłłs had issued large numbers of leases to poor

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 293
text:
Lithuanian nobles and boyars on terms which required them to turn out if required for war, suitably armed, or for sessions of the Sejm. These men could be raised in the short term by magnates; indeed it was one way in which the Commonwealth tried to mobilize quickly for war, but they were more an untrained militia than a proper army, and no magnate was in a state to maintain or pay such forces unless they were swiftly placed on the Commonwealth's payroll. Many of the supposedly 'private' troops at the royal elections of 1632 and 1669 were in all probability part of the regular army: in 1632 Krzysztof II Radziwiłł and Stanisław Koniecpolski were respectively grand hetmans of Lithuania and Poland, while in 1669 Michał Kazimierz Radziwiłł was Lithuanian grand hetman, Mikołaj Kazimierz Pac was Lithuanian field hetman, Jan Sobieski was Polish grand hetman and Dymitr Wiśniowiecki was Polish field hetman. In 1631, a year before the election to which he is supposed to have brought 10,000 men, Krzysztof II Radziwiłł's infantry numbered a princely 59 men. It is claimed that the size of these 'private armies' grew rapidly into the eighteenth century, but wild estimates do not accord with reality. Hieronim Florian Radziwiłł, who decided to establish a private army on his return from his Grand Tour in 1735, was estimated to have maintained a force of 6–10,000 men; the documents reveal that at its height, he managed to raise 1854 men, more than half of them irregular cossacks; after his death in 1760, it was reduced to 545 men by his successor, Michał Kazimierz Radziwiłł. For all their fabulous wealth, even the greatest Polish-Lithuanian magnates could not really compete with the State in military terms, even one so weakened by the eighteenth century as the Commonwealth; at best, they were more akin to clan chiefs in the Scottish Highlands who could raise a couple of thousand retainers in time of need, than German princes with properly-organised modern forces. Those that tried too hard were likely merely to compound their economic difficulties: rental rolls, especially in a system so dominated by serfdom, simply could not compete with taxation income, however large the estates.

Indeed, by the eighteenth century, many of the greater landholders had leased out or mortgaged large parts of their estates. Mortgaging was a useful way of raising loans, but the Commonwealth's high interest rates submerged many wealthy nobles in a deepening slough of debt. One study of landholding patterns in what is now central and western Belarus on the basis of hearth-tax registers reveals that although Karol Radziwiłł nominally owned 35,800 hearths in 1790 (14 per cent of the total for this area), less than a third (10,700) were in his direct control. Of 32 properties he inherited in the district of Nowogród, twenty had already been mortgaged in the early eighteenth century; by 1776, only one was left unmortgaged. Radziwiłł blamed the sequestration of his lands in 1764–67 and 1769–76 for his problems; the rest of the family blamed his prodigality. Although it is certainly true that Karol was – to put it mildly – an undistinguished and incompetent sprig of the mighty Radziwiłł tree, he was by no means the only magnate faced with

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 294
text:
such problems; they resulted more from the structure of landholding than the thirst for expensive Western luxuries which so many historians have stressed.

It is true that once a family was established at the peak of noble society any decline tended to be relative. There were ways to stave off disaster, or at least to preserve one's position. The property rights enjoyed by women meant that one option was to marry, although marriage could pose threats of its own. In 1642 Stanisław Lubomirski (1583–1649), divided his eighteen towns, 316 villages and 163 estates between his three sons, although the death of the youngest in 1663 saw his share divided between his brothers. The younger surviving brother, Jerzy Sebastian, managed eventually to build up his holdings to 229 villages and towns, but that included several starosties which he lost on his impeachment in 1664. He had, however, five sons and two daughters from two marriages, which caused the subdivision of his estates, a blow from which the junior line of the Lubomirskis never really recovered. The senior line was more fortunate: Aleksander Michał, Stanisław's eldest son, had only one child, Józef Karol, who married in 1683 the fabulously wealthy Teofilia Zasław-Ostrogska, heiress to the Ostrogski entail and the vast Zasławski fortune. On the death of Józef's only son in 1720, however, the estate went not to Jerzy Sebastian's descendants, but to Paweł Sanguszko, who married Józef's daughter Marianna. A match like this could transform a family's position. In 1724 Maria Zofia Sieniawska (1699–1771), heiress to the Sieniawski fortune, married Stanisław Denhoff, Lithuanian Field Hetman. On his death in 1728, she inherited his massive estate, which made her an even greater catch in 1731 for August Czartoryski, who had lost out to Sanguszko in the race for the Lubomirski inheritance, but now succeeded in establishing the financial basis which enabled the Czartoryskis – known as 'the Family' – to launch one of the most successful attempts ever by a magnate faction to dominate central politics.

Such transactions only benefited a handful, however; since wealthy heiresses were in short supply, competition for their favours was fierce and occasionally bloody. Most had to look elsewhere to maintain their position. The important role played by royal land in sustaining magnate incomes meant that even well-established families required access to starosties to provide for their heirs and to compensate for the effects of partible inheritance. This in itself was a source of intense instability, since so much of the monarchy's influence – and many of its problems – derived from the fact that, as with office, demand far outstripped supply: the tariff of 1771 listed a mere 1400 separate royal estates and leaseholds of various kinds (excluding Lithuania). The king did not enjoy complete freedom of action. Unlike public office, it was possible to cede a starosty, a practice that became increasingly common in the seventeenth century when a lively trade developed, with large sums of money changing hands for agreements to resign in favour: in 1660, Tobiasz Morsztyn ceded the starosty of Ostrołęka in Mazovia to Stefan Kazimierz

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 295
text:
Piaseczyński for 15,000 zloties. Fathers would attempt to secure their sons' futures by obtaining cessions on key royal estates in their possession before they died. Some families were thus able to avoid the worst consequences of subdivision, and individual starosties could become all but hereditary in certain families, at least for a period. In the eighteenth century the rich starosty of Hrubieszów in the palatinate of Ruthenia was held successively by Feliks Potocki, his son and grandson. Feliks's nephew Józef held three great starosties in the same palatinate (Leżajsk, Halicz and Śniatyrń). All three were passed on to his son, Stanisław, palatine of Poznań, who had to divide them since he had four sons, none of whom became a senator.

Nevertheless, if a tiny group of families undoubtedly grabbed more than its share of starosties, competition was so intense that the king had a great deal of room for manoeuvre. Despite the widespread practice of cession in favour, each transaction had to be confirmed by the royal chancery. Approval was usually forthcoming, even if payment in one form or another might be exacted. Nobody, however, could rely on passing on a starosty to their children, and starosties often passed out of the hands of families that had held them for a generation or more: the starosty of Bila Tserkva, the richest in the Commonwealth, was held successively by Jan Stanisław Jabłonowski, Polish Grand Hetman under John III Sobieski and Augustus II, and his son, Stanisław Wincenty, but on the latter's death in 1754 it was conferred on Jerzy Mniszech, despite the fact that Stanisław had a son, Antoni, who was allowed to keep two of his father's starosties, but lost Bila Tserkva, probably because of his father's long opposition to Augustus III.

Thus, for all the apparent advantages of the wealthiest groups in society, they never constituted a stable economic élite. Despite a dearth of studies, there is some evidence – not least the number of new men rising to senatorial rank throughout the period – to suggest that the middling nobility, while facing enormous problems between 1648 and 1721, was remarkably resilient. Contrary to the impression which is often given, the middle and lesser nobility held most of the cultivated land in private ownership: about 80 per cent in Great Poland at the end of the sixteenth century. One study of the district of Kalisz – which unfortunately only goes up to 1655 – suggests that the middle nobility devised strategies to avoid the worst effects of partible inheritance. Despite Kula's view that land was not a commodity, the land market was extremely lively, and although there was considerable activity by richer nobles, most transactions involved the middle nobility. A large number of sales took place within the family, as older siblings took advantage of their position to buy out the portions assigned to their younger brothers and ensure that divisions of the family property were limited or transient. The lack of studies of the economic activities of lesser landholders – particularly of those who leased or rented their lands – makes it difficult to reach firm conclusions, but it is clear that they were highly active economically: leases were often short, litigation was frequent and great effort had to be devoted to maintaining one's position.

title: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 296
text:
This may have been a defensive strategy, by which families ran hard to stay in the same place, but it left middling landowners in many respects better placed than many holders of debt-encrusted latifundia to profit from the improving economic conditions of the eighteenth century, as the internal market was stimulated after 1721 by a rising population, and foreign demand for Polish grain grew once more, albeit slowly. The rise in real prices stimulated a modest economic recovery, which was strongest in the western Polish lands, where the middle nobility was numerous and well placed to benefit from the Vistula export-trade. The buoyancy of the economy in these areas was demonstrated by the scale of settlement from abroad: between 1721 and 1793, some 775 new settlements with about 12,700 new households were established in Great Poland.

Despite the apparent dominance of the political system by wealthy nobles, the views of lesser nobles could not be ignored, since the Commonwealth's constitutional structure after 1569 ensured that szlachta of the meaner sort enjoyed political influence substantially beyond their economic power. Interest in politics remained high: it is estimated that nearly half the adult male nobility of Royal Prussia took an active part in political life in the mid-eighteenth century. Mazovia, where magnate estates were virtually unknown, had a large number of sejmiki to match its numerous nobility; it therefore sent proportionally more envoys to the Sejm than other, wealthier provinces: until 1764, almost one-sixth (30 out of 182) of the Chamber of Envoys, excluding those from Royal Prussia, were from the palatinates of Mazovia, Rawa and Plock. If the poor nobility were often unable to leave their plots of land to travel to the general Mazovian Sejmik, they enthusiastically attended district sejmiki, and smallholders were by no means excluded from serving as envoys or deputies. Moreover, Warsaw, where royal elections took place and where the vast majority of Sejm sessions were held after 1569, was the capital of Mazovia, and Mazovians therefore did not have far to travel to attend. Traditionally, Mazovians were presented by Polish historians as rather primitive and limited in their political outlook, but more recent work has stressed the full engagement of Mazovians with the political ideals of the Commonwealth, stressing their intrinsic legalism. While Mazovian envoys to the Sejm could be unruly, and their attachment to the ideals of the Commonwealth meant that they were intrinsically hostile to any royal plans which seemed to threaten the introduction of absolutum dominium, they were broadly regalist in outlook and could often be relied on to oppose the pretensions of magnate factions: thus although the Mazovians opposed John Casimir's plans to introduce an election vivente rege in 1661–62, they overwhelmingly supported him against Jerzy Sebastian Lubomirski in the crisis which ended in Lubomirski's rokosz (rebellion) of 1665–66. In royal elections, from 1573, when Mazovians played a central role in the election of Henry duke of Anjou, their influence was important. In 1669, a massive turnout of the ordinary nobility – some talked of 80,000

title_en: The Nobility of Poland–Lithuania, 1569–1795
label: p. 297
text:
being present – ensured the election of a native candidate, Michael Korybut Wiśniowiecki, in protest against the machinations of the great magnate factions, each manoeuvering to elect their own favoured foreigner. In 1674, when many Mazovians stayed away, it was a French-backed faction-leader – John Sobieski – who was elected. Even in Lithuania, traditionally seen as dominated by magnate clientes, the middling and lesser nobility in the first half of the seventeenth century demonstrated its clear attachment to the political ideals of the Commonwealth, and a willingness to act independently – or at least to manoeuvre to its own advantage between the magnate factions.

While the ordinary nobility had always been suspicious of royal reform initiatives which might threaten szlachta liberties, it by no means looked favourably on magnate behaviour, despite outward deference. Indeed, the growth in magnate power brought an increasing assertiveness from the mid-seventeenth century, in which the ordinary nobility sought to safeguard egalitarian principles. The ideals of the Execution Movement were not forgotten, and there was a constant strain of anti-magnate feeling within political life: during the crisis of the 1650s there were strong attacks on the system of distributing royal land, which was seen as responsible for civil strife and government poverty. The 1660s saw several attempts to subordinate the Senate to the Chamber of Envoys, while a clause in Wiśniowiecki's 1669 pacta conventa (election charter) banned more than one government minister per family. When the 1690 hearth tax statute referred to the 'lesser nobility' it provoked a storm, and the offending word was struck out in 1699 as violating szlachta equality. In Lithuania, where the Sapieha family did manage briefly to establish a dictatorial grip on politics in the latter period of Sobieski's reign, the middling szlachta exercised a vicious revenge after the Sapieha forces were destroyed at the battle of Olkieniki in 1700, slaughtering Michał Sapieha in cold blood and destroying the Sapieha hegemony forever. Magnates might still be able to appeal to noble solidarity in the name of szlachta republicanism, but they could not presume too much.

This was no oligarchy. There was no stable élite and success was dependent on conflict, not cooperation. Competition for heiresses, office, starosties and political influence was rife; rivalry was bitter and occasionally murderous. No one faction, or coalition of factions, could control central politics or access to patronage; indeed only the loose coalitions which formed royal support came close, but although the king could manoeuvre effectively among the great factions, using his control of patronage, he could not break free of reliance upon them: support of one led to the alienation of its rivals, and he could always be frustrated by szlachta suspicion of royal intentions and opposition groups which exploited the Commonwealth's decentralized political structure, or looked to foreign rulers who were only too eager to masquerade as protectors of the republican constitution. While the rebellions of Zebrzydowski in 1606–07 and Jerzy Sebastian Lubomirski in 1665–66,
